en: In earlier lectures, we already saw that you
can import HTML files into your Bun-powered
TypeScript or JavaScript files. And if you
do that, you're importing a BunHTMLBundle
object.
And you could use that either directly as a
value in that Bun web server router,
or you could access a.index property to get
the path to that file to then, for example,
read it with Bunfile.
Now, turns out that Bun allows you to import
other types of files as well, and that's
what we'll take a closer look at right now.
For example, you can import.toml,.json
files,
also HTML files in a different way as raw
text if you need that, and a bunch of other
file types.
Now, why is that interesting? Why would you
do that? Here I got a new simple demo
application and you find it attached, and
this is an invoice generator. Application.
This application comes with one dependency,
Playwright,
which is a browser automation tool which
could be used for end-to-end testing but
also for
simply spinning up a browser and then doing
something in it programmatically. And in
this application, I'm using Playwright to
spin up a little Chromium browser, which I
then only use to actually render out PDF
pages, my PDF invoices. And I'll get back to
the details of how this application works in
just a second. But if you installed all
dependencies and for Playwright, you also
will need to run this command here to make
sure that this Chromium browser is
available. So once you ran these commands,
you can run
bun run generate and that will run this Bun
script and generate some invoices. And it
will generate those invoices based on an
invoice template, which is set up here. And
you'll get some PDF files which are
generated with help of Playwright. So that's
essentially a web page, our HTML page that's
generated by the Bun app, then saved as a
PDF. And that's what I'm using Playwright
for. But
that's not the main thing here. And as
mentioned, I'll get back to the details of
how this application works. The main thing
for now is that you can import different
file types here. And why are we doing that?
Well, because for an application like this,
a little utility tool built with done,
you may need configuration files. For
example, for this invoice generator, you
might want a global or a central
company.toml file that contains your
company's data so that if you were to share
that invoice generator with someone else,
they could enter their invoice data, their
company data there. So their company name,
address, and so on.
You also might want a separate configuration
file which then contains invoice-specific
information and configuration like the tax
rate to apply.
And of course, we could merge this all into
one config file, but that's not the main
point here. The main point is when you're
building applications, you'll sometimes work
with configuration files that may be in JSON
or in TOML format or that may also be in
YAML format, which would also be supported
by Bun. And here for this demo, I'm simply
using TOML and JSON.
And Bun makes importing and using such
configuration files
because as mentioned and as shown here, you
can directly import TOML and JSON files. And
what you then do
is you add these little annotations with,
and then an object where you set the type to
TOML or the type to JSON, or if it were a
YAML file, you would set it to YAML, but
here it's TOML. And this annotation is just
here to give Bun some extra information
about what that file will include.
So what are we getting here with those
imports then? Well, company and config in
the end are objects. And for config, for
example, we can see that we're mapping this
to an InvoiceConfig type down here using
TypeScript's typeof operator. So the nice
thing about importing JSON with this
annotation here is that TypeScript is able
to understand this and we're able to infer
the types here. And we see that we'll have a
currency key, a locale key, and so on. And
these are simply the keys I have in this
JSON file. So we got TypeScript support for
that even though it's not defined in a
TypeScript file but in a JSON file. But
thanks to this import, we can infer the
actual types that are in that file from
there.
And if I were to add a new
key here in that JSON file, something
hello,
if I were to do that and I go to index.ts,
you will see that is now part of that
inferred type too. So that's pretty nice and
that's one reason why this import feature
provided by Bun here can be very useful. And
this invoice config is then simply used here
to build the invoice in the end and for
example set the currency that's showing up
there. And all that company data that's
coming from that company.toml file is in the
end merged and inserted into the invoice
HTML file because in that HTML file,
which we are also importing here, I'll get
back to that in a second. In that HTML file
I get some placeholders for company name,
address, and tax ID and so on.
Now that's of course the data we have in a
company TOML file
and that's why this company object that's
being imported here is in the end passed to
render template, which is a function that's
responsible for
filling the concrete data into that template
HTML file, which I just showed you.
So into that invoice HTML file per invoice
we're generating. And therefore what our
code here in the end does is it simply takes
a look at the key value pairs in that TOML
file and looks for placeholders with these
key names in that invoice template file. So
company name,
address, email,
that's what it's looking for.
And it fills in these values.
That's what we're doing with that imported
TOML file. And that invoice template here,
so that invoice HTML file, which I have in
my
templates folder here, that is also being
imported as a.html file. So similar to what
we saw in that web app from the last
lectures, but now also with this extra
annotation. And this annotation, just like
these annotations, that's not just cosmetic.
Instead, this also controls which file
loader will be used by Bun under the hood.
Now it infers a default file loader from the
extension. So for HTML, for example, the
default file loader used is an HTML loader,
which gives you that HTML bundle object as
an import And that's useful if you, for
example, want to access this index property,
which is the path to the file.
But you can also deliberately set a
different loader. Here I'm using the text
loader and that tells Bun to import this
HTML file as raw text. So instead of giving
you that HTML bundle object, it gives you
raw text. Now TypeScript here, at least when
I'm recording this, actually infers the
wrong type. HTML bundle. But actually what
we get here is a string, which is why I have
this line of code here where I explicitly
cast this to be of type string. So I'm
overriding the inferred TypeScript type
because this text loader will ensure that we
get a string, not an HTML bundle.
And I'm doing that here because I don't care
about the path of that HTML file or anything
like that. I'm just interested in the raw
text, the raw HTML code in there because
this invoice template is then passed to
render template
as a string. And then in there we simply go
through all the placeholders. This code
looks pretty complex, but we're just looking
for all these placeholders with the double
curly braces
and we're replacing them with the actual
values from the different config files we're
reading. That's what we're doing here when
we render that template. So this weird
looking regular expression just looks for
the curly braces with of various
key names between. That's what's happening
here.
And therefore, being able to import all
these different file types makes building
utility tools like this here, but also web
applications or any other kind of
application easier because you don't have to
manually parse these files. You don't have
to import third-party libraries that help
with parsing TOML files or anything like
that. Instead, Bun has it built in.
